title: Central and Eastern Europe’s Premier Free Knowledge Conference Debuts in Romania: Wikimedia CEE Meeting 2026 to Convene in Cluj-Napoca
content:
CLUJ-NAPOCA, Romania — For the first time in its history, Romania will host the annual regional conference of the Wikipedia movement: Wikimedia CEE Meeting 2026. Taking place from September 18 to 20, 2026, at Babeș-Bolyai University in Cluj-Napoca, the meeting brings together digital rights advocates, researchers, open-knowledge contributors, and chapter delegates from across Central and Eastern Europe and surrounding regions.

The event is organised by Wikimedians of Romania and Moldova User Group in partnership with Făgăraș Research Institute and hosted by Babeș-Bolyai University through its Faculty of European Studies, Office for Open Science, Centre for Students with Disabilities, and the Doctoral School “History. Culture. Civilisation.”

What is the Wikimedia CEE Meeting?

title: Growing from Wiki Club to Becoming a Community Towards the Future
content:
Reflections on the Wikimedia Malaysia 2026 Strategic Direction Conference

After discovering the Wikimedia platform, I began my journey of promoting and preserving my community’s language, Kadazandusun, through my participation in Wiki Club Kent. The club gave me an opportunity to learn more about the Wikimedia movement and to contribute to the world of free knowledge.

Today, that journey continues with the same mission. Although my time as a student and as a Wiki Club member has come to an end, my passion for contributing remains. I hope to take the Kadazandusun language further into the world as part of this community.

On 30th August 2026, I had the opportunity to participate in the Malaysian Wikimedia Strategy Summit 2026 in Kuala Lumpur, which brought together Wikimedians and community leaders from diverse backgrounds across Malaysia. For me, this was more than just a conference. It was a space for us to pause, reflect on the journey we have taken so far, and envision where the Malaysian Wikimedia community wants to go next.

title: Women, the Sundanese Language, and Wikimedia Projects
content:
In our daily life, there are things we do not notice while they are still around us. A mother tongue can be one of them. We grow up hearing it at home, in conversations with family,  jokes exchanged between neighbours, or stories told before bedtime. We rarely stop to think about how many of our memories are carried by the words we inherit. However, when those words begin to disappear, we do realize that a language is never simply a collection of vocabulary, It is a way of remembering who we are.

I am a Sundanese woman, and Sundanese is part of the memory. 

For me, the question of whether the Sundanese language will continue to live is not merely a linguistic question. It is a deeply personal one. It is connected to the kind of world we will leave behind for the generations that come after us. Will they still be able to read old expressions, understand the stories told by their grandparents, recognize the names of plants and places in their own language? Or they simply have the freedom to say, “This is my language.”

Weekly highlight

  • The Future Audiences team has started a discussion on English Wikipedia about a proposed new experiment to show a temporary notice about the new Google Preferred Sources feature to Wikipedia readers coming from Google. The experiment is to test whether this notice makes visitors come back to Wikipedia more often. Preferred Sources feature lets users choose websites they trust so Google can highlight content from those sources more prominently in Search and AI experiences. We are interested in testing this on other languages that Google supports and would welcome assistance with starting conversations on other wikis. If interested, please reach out to Future Audiences on the talk page.

title: CEE Beyond the Crossroads: Wikimedia CEE Meeting 2026 Convenes in Cluj-Napoca
content:
From September 18 to 20, 2026, Wikimedians, open-knowledge researchers, and free-culture advocates from Central and Eastern Europe—and increasingly Central Asia—gather for the first time in Cluj-Napoca, Romania, for the Wikimedia CEE Meeting 2026. 

Hosted by Wikimedians of Romania and Moldova User Group in partnership with Făgăraș Research Institute and Babeș-Bolyai University (UBB), this year’s regional conference marks a defining step forward for one of the most interconnected community networks in the Wikimedia movement. 

Under the slogan “CEE Beyond the Crossroads,” the meeting signals a profound shift: moving past reactive survival amid geopolitical and digital fragmentation toward long-term regional resilience, institutional empowerment, and intentional cooperation.

title: African Wikipedian Alliance (AWA) Fellowship Reflections: Learning Through Pan-Africanism by Daniel Damilola Obiokeke
content: I began the African Wikipedian Alliance European Partnership for Democracy Digital Democracy Initiative (EPD-DDI) Enhancing Youth Voices and Youth Civic Engagement in a Secured Digital Space through it Digitise Youth fellowship thinking I already understood the terrain. I had worked in Wikimedia spaces before, led communities, and supported projects that reached beyond Nigeria, so I assumed this experience would mainly extend across my technical process for finding topics, identifying red links, and guiding contributors toward strong articles. What I did not expect was that the deepest lesson of the fellowship would not be about editing tools at all. It would be about how knowledge moves across Africa, and how often that movement is interrupted by language, sourcing barriers, and the unequal conditions under which some references are required to be documented.

title: “We mostly do this stuff just for the love of it”: WikiCelebrating Juan “BugWarp” Kulichevsky
content:
We are proud to WikiCelebrate Juan Kulichevsky today, known across Wikimedia projects as User:BugWarp. Juan has contributed to Wikimedia projects since childhood and is passionate about sports photography, free knowledge, and community building in Argentina and beyond.

Juan’s Wikimedia journey began in a pretty unusual way when he was just 10 years old.

“It’s quite funny actually, if you look at my account, I’ve been registered since July 2009. I was only 10 years old then! Already back then we used Wikipedia a lot with my friends at school so we could finish our homework,” Juan remembers. Inspired after a friend’s father donated to Wikipedia, Juan decided the “coolest thing” he could do was create an account himself.

“Little did I know that this would be the start of something great. Many years later, I remembered that you can freely contribute to the project, and I started uploading pictures to Commons of people and things that weren’t available on Wiki, and then I took the courage to start editing and writing articles.” Juan says.

Today, much of his work focuses on sports photography and improving the visual representation of athletes across Wikimedia projects.

title: From Focus Group to Skills Focus: A New Programme of Wiki Loves Women
content:
As we continue celebrating 10 years of Wiki Loves Women, we are looking not only at what has been achieved, but also at how the initiative continues to grow and create new opportunities for communities. After celebrating a decade of making women more visible through initiatives such as SheSaid, ISA Campaign, Wiki OTO, we are turning the spotlight to another part of the initiative: building skills through learning and doing.

In 2026, Wiki Loves Women launched the Skills Focus Programme, a practical, group based online training programme designed to help Wikimedia and Open movement community members develop specific skills through hands-on learning and creation. Each cohort explores one theme, bringing together participants from all the genders to learn, practise, and work towards a tangible final output.

title: From Partnership to Platform: How EduWiki Hub and Capacity Exchange Are Creating Better “Pathways to Mentorship”
content:
What happens when a community that knows what people need meets a platform designed to help people share what they know?

For EduWiki Hub and Capacity Exchange (CapX), the answer has been a partnership that has grown from an idea into something practical: a more connected way for Wikimedians to find mentors, share skills, and contribute to the growth of others across the Movement.

Our collaboration began early in the development of the EduWiki Hub and continued through our first mentorship cohort. But it was during the development of our second cohort that the partnership really started to take shape.

Instead of relying on external tools such as Google Forms, we worked together to bring the EduWiki Mentorship Program directly into Capacity Exchange. EduWiki Hub brought the program model, community knowledge, outreach, and understanding of the skills and support our participants needed. CapX brought the technical infrastructure and worked with us to turn those needs into a functioning platform.

title: One Movement, Many Voices: My Experience at the Malaysian Wikimedia Strategy Summit
content:
When I arrived at the Malaysian Wikimedia Strategy Summit on 29 August 2026, one of the first things I noticed was how familiar and unfamiliar the Wikimedia community could feel at the same time.

I met again with Wikimedians whom I had not seen in a while, while also getting to know new members of the community. Seeing familiar faces again while meeting new people reminded me that the Wikimedia community is constantly growing, while the friendships formed through Wikimedia activities can continue even after an event ends.

But as the day went on, I realized that the summit was about much more than simply bringing Wikimedians together. It gave us an opportunity to think about where the Wikimedia movement in Malaysia is going, what challenges we face, and what role each of us can play in shaping its future.

title: “WikiGameJam: Developing Wiki Games from Coast to Coast”
content:
The Wikimedia community has a long history of community-built games powered by Wikipedia and other Wikimedia projects. The Wiki Arcade website showcases many of these games, from WikiAsteroids (arcade space-shooter powered by Wikipedia’s recent changes) to Redactle (guess the article from hidden words) to Catfishing (guess the Wikipedia articles based on categories).

There’s a lot of untapped creative energy around wiki-based games, both from people already building playful experiments on top of Wikipedia, as teaching projects and from the broader game dev community.  To channel that, we launched WikiGameJam: an event and space for people to turn that playful spirit into new and exciting wiki games. The goal is to build on the ways people already engage with Wikipedia, as a trivia trove, a creative rabbit hole, or a challenge to race from one article to another.

We hosted the first-ever WikiGameJam on October 3–5, 2025, in Brooklyn, New York City. The weekend hackathon brought together developers, designers, and Wikipedia enthusiasts to collaborate and build new games powered by Wikipedia, Wikidata, and other Wikimedia projects.

title: Making space for Sylheti: From a decade-long Wikipedia journey to Wiki Loves Sylotology
content:
Sylheti Wikipedia began as a long-term effort to create a space for a language that had been largely absent from the digital knowledge ecosystem. More than a decade after the first proposal, the project has grown into something broader: a community movement connecting language preservation, education, local history and open knowledge.

On 25 February 2025, the Sylheti Wikipedia officially became available to the public. For many people, the launch of a new Wikipedia language edition might appear to be a technical milestone: a new website, a new language code, and a growing collection of articles. For the Sylheti community, however, the moment represented something much larger.

It marked the culmination of a journey that had begun more than a decade earlier, when Wikimedians started working towards creating a digital knowledge platform for the Sylheti language. The proposal for Sylheti Wikipedia had begun in 2014, and after years of community-driven work, the Wikimedia Foundation approved the project on 14 February 2025. The Wikipedia officially launched shortly afterwards, using the traditional Sylheti Nagri script.

title: Nurturing the Community: Reflections on Attending Code4Lib Japan 2026
content: I attended the Code4Lib Japan Conference 2026, held on September 6–7, 2026. Code4Lib, established in 2003, is a community centered on library-related programmers and systems engineers, primarily active in the United States. Participation from Japan began in 2010, leading to the formation of Code4Lib Japan by those early participants. In Japan, the community is open not only to technical experts but also to librarians in general. Conferences have been held annually since 2013; this year marked the 14th conference, which took place over two days at Kogakkan University in Ise City, Mie Prefecture.
